## Proof

**Claim.** The only entire function $f$ satisfying $f(x)=e^x$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$ is $f(z)=e^z$.

**Proof.** Let $f$ be an entire function with $f(x)=e^x$ for every real number $x$. Define
$$g(z) := f(z) - e^z.$$
Since $f$ is entire and $e^z$ is entire, $g$ is entire (holomorphic on all of $\mathbb{C}$).

For every $x\in\mathbb{R}$,
$$g(x) = f(x) - e^x = e^x - e^x = 0.$$
Thus $g$ vanishes on the entire real axis $\mathbb{R}\subset\mathbb{C}$.

The real axis has an accumulation point in $\mathbb{C}$: for instance, $0$ is an accumulation point of $\mathbb{R}$, since every neighborhood of $0$ contains infinitely many real numbers (indeed $1/n\to 0$).

By the **Identity Theorem** for holomorphic functions: if two functions holomorphic on a connected open set agree on a subset that has an accumulation point within that set, then they agree everywhere on the set.

Applying this to $g$ (which is holomorphic on the connected open set $\mathbb{C}$) and the zero function: $g$ vanishes on $\mathbb{R}$, which has an accumulation point $0\in\mathbb{C}$, so $g\equiv 0$ on $\mathbb{C}$.

Therefore
$$f(z) - e^z = 0 \quad\text{for all } z\in\mathbb{C},$$
i.e.,
$$f(z) = e^z \quad\text{for all } z\in\mathbb{C}.$$

**Conclusion.** Yes, $f(z)=e^z$ is the only entire function agreeing with $e^x$ on the real line. The key point is that the real axis is a set with accumulation points inside the domain $\mathbb{C}$, so the Identity Theorem forces uniqueness. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
